newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr revives as Japan rates subside.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr revives as Japan rates subside.

text.p: The Australian dollar rallied 1/3 cent Wednesday as unlooked for weakness in the Japanese economy promised to keep rates there at record lows for months yet.

That should sustain Japanese investor demand for high yielding A$ samurai bonds and, in turn, the currency, analysts said. For those with farther horizons, however, the prospect of a sluggish Japan boded ill for the commodity price cycle.
"The rate implications are positive, but on a broad view its hard to see how a slow Japan fits into the commodity boom bulls are betting on," said Macquarie Bank economist Richard Gibbs.
By 5.00 pm (0630 GMT) the local currency had bounced to US$0.7905/10 after dipping as far as US$0.7867/72 ahead of the Japanese news, and was up on Tuesday's late US$0.7888/93.
The bounce reduced the risk of another retreat to US$0.7810 support, but dealers reckoned the currency still needed to clear US$0.7935 resistance to restore confidence in its uptrend.
On the crosses it leapt to 85.67/77 yen from Tuesday's late 84.90/00 and firmed to 57.8 in trade weighted terms from 57.7.
"A lot of people got short AUD/yen and were buried," said a local bank dealer. "I was just as bearish, but now that Japanese inflows look assured you've got to say its going higher."

The dollar had come under pressure this week as the market cut short yen positions in case the Tankan survey of business conditions proved stronger than expected and hastened the tightening of monetary policy.

There were even rumours the main index would rise as far as +5, so the actual result came as a big relief to dollar holders. The Bank of Japan's diffusion index for large manufacturers fell to -7.0 in the August quarter, from -3.0 in Q2, when the market had been looking for an improvement to around +1.0. This index measures the percentage of firms which expect business conditions to improve minus those who expect it to worsen.
There was some progress in investment intentions for 1996/97 with major firms expecting a 6.6 percent rise in capital spending, up from 6.0 percent in the previous survey.
"Private investment will somewhat offset the unwinding of public spending, but the authorities cannot be comfortable where the economy is heading," said Macquarie's Gibbs.
"It's positive for the AUD short term as it dispells any lingering concern about a Japanese rate hike,' said Gibbs.
The market certainly agreed as the key December three month Euro-yen contract leapt 17 basis points to 99.31, implying a rate of 0.70 percent compared to the current ODR of 0.5 percent.
The comparable A$ contract currently stands at 93.25 implying a rate of 6.75 percent.
Such a healthy premium had attracted huge demand for A$ saumrai bonds this year from Japanese retail investors.
Analysts saw little reason why that should in the near term, particularly as offshore confidence in Australia had been boosted by last week's tight Federal budget.

However, there were reservations on the medium term outlook given that much of the bullish sentiment for the currency had been predicated on a strong, synchronised upturn in world growth and commodity prices in late 1996 and 1997.

"A sluggish Japan does not augur well for a strong commodity price cycle," said Gibbs. "Less growth in Japan means less growth in East Asia, and that's on top of uncertainty in Germany and core Europe."
Commodity price trends are a major driving force behind the Australian dollar as commodities make up over 60 percent of the country's exports.

Today's domestic data were completely overshadowed by the events in Jpaan, but the foreign investment figures did support the Australian government's drive for fiscal prudence as set out in last week's tight 1996/97 budget.
Australia was in debt to the tune of A$187.804 billion in the June quarter, up from A$185.155 in Q1 but much in line with market forecasts.
The ratio of net debt to GDP inched down to 38.6 from 38.7 in the March quarter, continuing the improvement seen since 1992/93 when it topped 41 percent.

Australia's ability to service its debt also improved with the percentage of export earnings needed to make interest payments falling to 11.3 percent from 11.9 in Q1 and more than 20.0 percent in 1989/90.
